summary.text: Diffraction is the bending and spreading of waves when they meet an obstacle or pass through an opening, with no change in their energy.
It is the same effect as interference, but the word is used when many waves are superposed, and it is explained by treating each point on a wavefront as a source of small spherical wavelets.
It shows up in security devices on credit cards and in methods for finding the atomic structure of materials.

facts.label: First recorded
facts.value: Francesco Maria Grimaldi observed it accurately in 1660

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Latin diffringere, meaning to break into pieces

facts.label: Who diffracts
facts.value: All waves, including water, sound and gravitational waves

facts.label: Shadow surprise
facts.value: Light appears behind a circular obstruction

items.prompt: You shine a bright lamp at a coin and look very closely at the edge of its shadow. What do you find?

options.label: A perfectly crisp dark edge, just as straight rays predict
An edge that is not crisp, because waves interfere beyond the obstacle
A glowing halo caused by the coin heating up
No shadow at all, because light bends fully around objects

items.explain: A strong light blocked by a solid object does not show a perfectly crisp shadow, since waves beyond the obstacle interfere.

items.prompt: In 1818 Poisson tried to sink Fresnel's wave theory with a prediction that sounded absurd. What was it, and how did it turn out?

options.label: Light in the middle of a circular shadow; an experiment found it
A dark spot in the middle of a bright beam; no one could find it
Light moving faster through a slit; tests showed it did not
Colors splitting inside a shadow; no one could reproduce it

items.explain: Poisson showed the theory predicted light in the shadow behind a circular obstruction, and Arago then showed experimentally that this light is visible, confirming Fresnel.

items.prompt: Using the Huygens-Fresnel picture, what happens when an obstacle blocks part of a wavefront?

options.label: The whole wave stops
The remaining wavelets turn into particles
The blocked wavelets pass through the obstacle anyway
The remaining wavelets also spread into the area behind the obstacle

items.explain: The unblocked secondary waves continue the wavefront and also create waves behind the obstacle, forming the diffraction pattern.

items.prompt: A few waves overlap in one setup; thousands overlap after passing a narrow gap in another. How do physicists treat these?

options.label: As two unrelated effects that only look alike on a screen
As sound versus light, which follow quite different rules
As the same effect, with a different name depending on how many waves overlap
As an effect that only matter waves such as electrons can show

items.explain: Diffraction is the same physical effect as interference; the term interference is usually used for a few waves and diffraction for many.

items.prompt: You replace one opening in a barrier with several openings very close together. What happens to the pattern?

options.label: It becomes a single bright spot
A more complex pattern of varying intensity can appear
It disappears because less light gets through
It becomes evenly bright across the screen

items.explain: Multiple closely spaced openings can produce a complex pattern of varying intensity.

items.prompt: Thomas Young looked at the fringes behind an illuminated sharp edge. How did he explain them?

options.label: Interference between the direct wave and a wave that seems to come from the edge
Tiny light particles bouncing off the sharp edge itself
Heat rising from the edge and bending the nearby light
Light being absorbed unevenly by the material of the barrier

items.explain: Young proposed that the fringes came from interference between the direct transmitted plane wave and a cylindrical wave that appears to be emitted from the edge.

paragraphs.heading: What diffraction is
paragraphs.text: Diffraction is what happens when a wave stops travelling in a straight line because it meets an obstacle or passes through an opening. The wave keeps the same energy. It happens whenever a wave runs into some kind of obstruction. That obstruction may block the wave completely, or it may be transparent and simply shift the wave's phase. Diffraction is really the same effect as interference: the word interference tends to be used when a few waves combine, and diffraction when many do.

paragraphs.heading: Wavelets and patterns
paragraphs.text: The simplest model is the Huygens–Fresnel principle. It treats every point on a wavefront as a source of a secondary spherical wave, called a Huygens wavelet. The Fresnel part adds these wavelets together and lets them interfere. When an obstacle blocks some of the wavelets, the rest carry the wave onward and also send waves behind the obstacle. Those waves build the diffraction pattern, a map of the directions the waves take after they have been diffracted.

paragraphs.heading: Bright and dark bands
paragraphs.text: The wavelets reach the screen by paths of different lengths, and the pattern comes from adding them all up. The sum of overlapping waves depends on their amplitudes and their relative phases, so the total can be anything from zero to the sum of the separate amplitudes. Where the phase difference is half a cycle, waves cancel each other out. That is why diffraction patterns usually show a series of maxima and minima. The straight-line paths of geometrical optics cannot predict such a pattern.

paragraphs.heading: All waves do it
paragraphs.text: Every kind of wave diffracts: water waves, sound, radio waves, X-rays, gravitational waves, and matter waves such as electrons and neutrons. The patterns are most pronounced when a coherent source such as a laser meets a slit. Several closely spaced openings can give a complex pattern of varying brightness. As a simple example, a strong light blocked by a solid object does not cast a crisp dark shadow when you look carefully. Diffraction plays a part in things as different as credit card security devices and methods for finding the atomic structure of materials at the nanoscale.

paragraphs.heading: Early observers
paragraphs.text: The Italian scientist Francesco Maria Grimaldi recorded accurate observations in 1660 and coined the word, from the Latin diffringere, "to break into pieces". His results were published in 1665, after his death. Isaac Newton studied the effects and attributed them to what he called the inflexion of light rays. James Gregory saw diffraction patterns made by a bird feather, in effect the first diffraction grating discovered. Thomas Young gave the first wave treatment of diffraction in 1800.

paragraphs.heading: The spot in the shadow
paragraphs.text: Augustin-Jean Fresnel later built an alternative wave theory on Huygens' principle. At first Young's model was considered incorrect, but later work showed the two approaches are equivalent. In 1818, supporters of the corpuscular, or particle, theory of light proposed diffraction as the Paris Academy prize question, expecting the wave theory to lose. When Fresnel's entry looked likely to win, Siméon Denis Poisson objected that the theory implied light should appear in the shadow behind a circular obstruction. Dominique-François-Jean Arago then showed by experiment that this light can be seen, confirming Fresnel's model.

paragraphs.heading: The quantum view
paragraphs.text: In quantum mechanics, diffraction is still described with a wave. Here, though, the wave function stands for a probability amplitude, and squaring its modulus gives the probability of detection. The light and dark parts of a diffraction pattern then become places where quanta are more or less likely to be detected.
